english: Really? — a polite check that you heard right, mild surprise or interest.
usage: polite -요, to anyone you'd use 존댓말 with
casual banmal, to a friend or younger person
fuller polite form, slightly stronger doubt
natural extension asking about a situation
examples: A: 나 합격했어 / B: 정말?
A: I passed / B: Really?
the bare one-word reaction — quick mild surprise
A: 이거 무료예요 / B: 정말요? 감사합니다!
A: This is free / B: Really? Thank you!
everyday: polite 정말요 to a stranger giving good news
A: 사장님이 오늘 일찍 보내준대 / B: 정말요? 웬일이래.
A: The boss says he'll let us off early / B: Really? What's gotten into him.
real situation: surprised but pleased reaction at work
nuance: 정말요? (polite) / 정말? (casual) is the everyday 'really?' you say to confirm you heard correctly, with light surprise or interest — not strong disbelief. It is built from 정말 'truly' plus the polite particle -요, so dropping the -요 makes it banmal: say plain 정말? to a friend, but to a boss, elder, or stranger you must keep 정말요? or you sound too familiar. The nearest alternative is 진짜요?, and the dividing line is register feel: 정말요? is the neutral, safe choice that works in any setting including formal ones, while 진짜? is more colloquial and casual. The English-speaker pitfall is intonation — Korean 'really?' MUST rise sharply at the end to read as a question; said flat, 정말요 turns into 'truly' as a statement and confuses the listener. Also, don't pile on 정말 진짜요? thinking it's stronger; pick one.

Saying it flat without rising intonation — 정말 with no upward pitch reads as the adverb 'truly,' not the question 'really?'; the pitch must rise.
Stacking 정말 진짜요? to sound more surprised — these are two words for the same thing; native speakers use one, not both together.

english: Really?! / for real? — surprised, more colloquial and emotional than 정말요.
usage: polite -요, casual-friendly tone with strangers your age
casual banmal, very common among friends
examples: A: 나 로또 됐어 / B: 진짜?!
A: I won the lottery / B: For real?!
the bare reaction — excited, can't-believe-it surprise
A: 그 식당 오늘 문 닫았어요 / B: 진짜요? 아쉽다.
A: That restaurant is closed today / B: Really? What a shame.
everyday: polite-casual 진짜요 to a coworker
A: 우리 팀 이겼대! / B: 진짜? 대박, 언제?
A: They say our team won! / B: For real? Awesome, when?
real situation: 진짜 flows straight into 대박 in excited chat
nuance: 진짜요? (polite) / 진짜? (casual) is the more emotional, colloquial cousin of 정말요? — it leaks more genuine surprise and excitement. It comes from 진짜 'real, genuine' (the 진 is the 한자 眞 'true') plus -요, so 진짜? alone is banmal and 진짜요? is the polite version. The dividing line versus 정말요? is tone and setting: 진짜? feels warmer, more spontaneous, and slightly more casual, so among friends it is the default, while in a stiff formal or business context 정말요? is safer because 진짜요? can sound a touch too relaxed. The English-speaker pitfall is register over-confidence: 진짜요? is polite-ish but still informal-flavored, so to a CEO, a much older stranger, or in a ceremony, the cleaner choice is 정말요? or 그래요?. Also, like all these, intonation must rise — flat 진짜 means 'genuinely / for real (emphasis),' not the question.

english: Awesome! / wow / no way — a big reaction to something amazing, shocking, or extreme.
usage: casual banmal, to friends, very common
examples: A: 나 승진했어 / B: 대박!
A: I got promoted / B: Awesome!
the bare slang reaction — pure excitement
A: 이 카페 디저트 봐 / B: 와, 대박이다.
A: Look at this cafe's dessert / B: Wow, that's amazing.
everyday: reacting to something impressive you see
A: 옆집에 불났대 / B: 헐, 대박. 다친 사람은 없대?
A: They say the next building caught fire / B: Whoa, no way. Anyone hurt?
real situation: 대박 also works for shocking-bad news, not just good
nuance: 대박 literally means 'a big hit / jackpot,' and as a reaction it explodes out for anything extreme — amazingly good, but also shocking or unbelievably bad. It is slang and firmly casual: 대박 alone is banmal among friends, and to add even a little politeness you say 대박이에요, though even that stays informal in flavor. The line against 헐 is direction: 헐 leans toward shock/dismay ('whoa, what?!'), while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's huge,' though both can overlap. Because it is young, casual slang, the English-speaker pitfall is using it with a boss, an elder, or in any formal setting — it sounds flippant and too street; there you'd say 정말 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요 instead. Another pitfall is assuming it's only positive; Koreans say 대박 at a car crash too, meaning 'unbelievable.'

Assuming 대박 is only for good news — it reacts to anything extreme, including shocking bad events; tone and context decide the meaning.
Adding -요 as 대박요 — that's not natural; the polite form is 대박이에요, since 대박 is a noun that needs the 이에요 copula.

english: Whoa / OMG / no way — a gut reaction of shock, disbelief, or mild dismay.
usage: casual banmal, friends and texting, very common
paired with 대박 for double shock
shock plus asking if it's true
oh no, what do we do
examples: A: 나 폰 잃어버렸어 / B: 헐.
A: I lost my phone / B: Whoa.
the bare interjection — instant shock
A: 시험이 내일이래 / B: 헐, 나 하나도 공부 안 했는데.
A: They say the exam is tomorrow / B: OMG, I haven't studied at all.
everyday: dismayed reaction to bad news
A: 걔네 헤어졌대 / B: 헐, 진짜? 왜?
A: They say those two broke up / B: Whoa, really? Why?
real situation: 헐 opens a surprised reaction, then you ask details
nuance: 헐 is a pure interjection of shock — the sound you make when something startling, dismaying, or unbelievable hits you, hugely common in texting and casual speech. It has no polite form because it's a raw exclamation; it lives entirely in banmal/casual territory among friends and peers. The dividing line versus 대박 is feeling: 헐 carries surprise often tinged with 'oh no' / dismay, while 대박 leans 'wow, that's huge' — that's why 헐 어떡해 (shock + worry) is natural but 대박 어떡해 is odd. The English-speaker pitfall is using it in any professional or respectful setting — to an elder or boss 헐 sounds childish and rude; there you'd react with 어머 (more neutral surprise) or a full 정말요? 그런 일이. Also don't write it as 헉 expecting the same thing — 헉 is a sharp gasp of fright, slightly different from the disbelieving 헐.

Mixing up 헐 and 헉 — 헐 is disbelief/dismay ('whoa, no way'), while 헉 is a startled gasp of fright; they aren't interchangeable.

english: Wow, that's cool / awesome — admiring something or someone impressive.
usage: with 진짜 to intensify the praise
examples: A: 나 마라톤 완주했어 / B: 와 멋있다!
A: I finished the marathon / B: Wow, that's awesome!
the bare admiring reaction — praising an achievement
A: 이 야경 좀 봐 / B: 와, 멋있다.
A: Look at this night view / B: Wow, that's gorgeous.
everyday: admiring a beautiful sight
A: 부장님이 영어로 발표하셨어 / B: 와, 멋있으시다.
A: The manager presented in English / B: Wow, that's so impressive of him.
real situation: honorific 멋있으시다 when praising a senior
nuance: 와 멋있다 is the spontaneous 'wow, that's cool / awesome' you exclaim at something or someone impressive — 와 is the gasp 'wow' and 멋있다 means 'is cool/stylish/admirable.' The plain 멋있다 is the casual exclamatory form (used even to oneself), 멋있어요 is polite, and to praise an elder or senior you add honorific -으시- → 멋있으시다/멋있으세요. The dividing line versus 예쁘다 ('pretty') and 대단하다 ('remarkable, impressive') is what you admire: 멋있다 is cool/stylish/admirable (a person's skill, a view, an attitude), 예쁘다 is cute/pretty (looks, small things), 대단하다 stresses achievement/effort. The English-speaker pitfall is the exclamatory -다 ending: learners think 멋있다 is dictionary form so they avoid saying it, but 멋있다! as a live reaction is completely natural and idiomatic. Another pitfall is praising a senior with plain 멋있어 — drop the honorific and it sounds over-familiar.

english: That's great / good for you / it worked out — happy something turned out well.
usage: that's great / glad it worked out
with 정말 to warm up the congratulation
examples: A: 나 그 회사 붙었어 / B: 잘됐다!
A: I got into that company / B: That's great!
the bare reaction — sharing someone's good news
A: 엄마 수술 잘 끝났어 / B: 아, 정말 잘됐다.
A: Mom's surgery went well / B: Oh, I'm so glad.
everyday: relief and happiness at good news
A: 비자 드디어 나왔어요 / B: 잘됐어요! 고생 많으셨어요.
A: My visa finally came through / B: That's wonderful! You worked so hard.
real situation: polite 잘됐어요 plus acknowledging their effort
nuance: 잘됐다 means 'it turned out well / that's great' — the warm reaction when something works out for someone (or yourself). It's 잘 'well' + 되다 'to turn out,' frozen as an exclamation: 잘됐다/잘됐어 casual, 잘됐어요 polite, 잘됐네(요) softly reacting to news. The dividing line versus 다행이다 is the feeling: 잘됐다 is 'good news, I'm happy for you' (a positive outcome), while 다행이다 is 'thank goodness, what a relief' (you were worried and it didn't go badly). A passed exam → 잘됐다; a near-miss accident with no injuries → 다행이다. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling/spacing: it's one word 잘됐다 (not 잘 됬다 — 됬다 is always wrong; the correct past of 되다 is 됐다). Another pitfall is mistaking it for sarcasm: said flat or with an eye-roll 잘됐다 can mean 'serves you right,' so keep your tone clearly warm.

Using 잘됐다 when you mean 'what a relief' — for a feared outcome that didn't happen use 다행이다; 잘됐다 is for genuinely good news.
Saying 잘됐다 flatly or with a sour tone — it can flip to sarcastic 'serves you right'; keep your voice warm so it reads as sincere congratulations.

english: Thank goodness / what a relief — relieved that something bad was avoided.
usage: casual with -네 on hearing reassuring news
examples: A: 검사 결과 괜찮대 / B: 다행이다.
A: The test results are fine / B: Thank goodness.
the bare reaction — pure relief
A: 지갑 택시에서 찾았어 / B: 아, 다행이다. 걱정했잖아.
A: I found my wallet in the taxi / B: Oh, what a relief. I was worried.
everyday: relief after a scare, with 걱정했잖아
A: 사고 났는데 다친 데는 없어요 / B: 다행이에요, 정말. 몸조심하세요.
A: There was an accident but no one's hurt / B: That's such a relief, really. Take care.
real situation: polite 다행이에요 reacting to a serious near-miss
nuance: 다행이다 is the 'thank goodness, what a relief' you breathe out when a feared bad outcome was avoided — built from the noun 다행 'good fortune/luck (that it wasn't worse)' + 이다. Casual is 다행이다/다행이야, polite is 다행이에요, and for a grave near-miss you intensify to 천만다행이다 'an immense relief.' The dividing line versus 잘됐다 is the emotional starting point: 다행이다 implies you were WORRIED and disaster was dodged, while 잘됐다 is plain happiness at good news with no prior dread — a clean bill of health you feared → 다행이다, a promotion you hoped for → 잘됐다. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'lucky' as 운이 좋다: 운이 좋다 is 'fortunate (won something, got a break),' but the relief that 'it could have been bad but wasn't' is specifically 다행이다. Another pitfall is forgetting the copula and saying 다행 alone — it needs 이다/이에요 to be a complete reaction.

Using 운이 좋다 ('lucky') for relief — 운이 좋다 means fortunate/got a break, but 'phew, it wasn't bad' is 다행이다, a different feeling.
Swapping in 잘됐다 — 잘됐다 is happiness at good news, while 다행이다 specifically means a feared bad outcome was avoided; the worry is the key difference.

english: What do I do? / oh no — distressed, not knowing how to handle a problem.
usage: what do I do? / oh no
what do I do / oh no
fuller form, asking for a real solution
examples: A: 마지막 버스 끊겼어 / B: 어떡해.
A: The last bus is gone / B: Oh no.
the bare reaction — dismay at a problem
A: 발표 자료를 안 가져왔어요 / B: 어떡해요, 지금 출력 가능해요?
A: I didn't bring the presentation file / B: Oh no, can you print it now?
everyday: dismay shading into problem-solving
A: 너 핸드폰 액정 깨졌어 / B: 헐, 어떡해, 이거 산 지 일주일 됐는데.
A: Your phone screen is cracked / B: OMG, oh no, I only bought it a week ago.
real situation: 어떡해 as pure distress, not literally asking 'how'
nuance: 어떡해(요) is the distressed 'oh no, what do I do?!' you blurt when a problem hits and you feel stuck — often it's an exclamation of dismay, not a literal request for instructions. It's the contracted spoken form of 어떻게 해 'how (shall I) do': casual 어떡해, polite 어떡해요. The critical dividing line is spelling: 어떡해 is the contraction you SAY ('what do I do'), while 어떻게 is the adverb 'how' that modifies a verb (어떻게 가요? 'how do I go?') — Koreans themselves mix these up in writing, but they are not interchangeable. The English-speaker pitfall is writing 어떻해 (a non-word) or using 어떻게 where the exclamation 어떡해 belongs. Another pitfall is register: 어떡해 is banmal, so to a boss or elder keep 어떡해요, or to genuinely ask for help say 어떻게 하면 좋을까요? Said softly to someone else's misfortune, 어떡해 also means sympathetic 'oh no, poor you.'

Using 어떻게 where you mean the dismay 'oh no' — 어떻게 is 'how' (어떻게 해요? = how do I do it), while the panicked exclamation is 어떡해(요).
Saying plain 어떡해 to a boss or elder — it's banmal; use 어떡해요, or to ask for actual help say 어떻게 하면 좋을까요?.

english: That's a shame / too bad / I wish it were different — mild regret or disappointment.
usage: casual with -네 reacting in the moment
it's a bit of a letdown
with 좀 to soften it further
examples: A: 표 다 팔렸대 / B: 아쉽다.
A: The tickets are all sold out / B: That's a shame.
the bare reaction — light disappointment
A: 저 다음 주에 이사 가요 / B: 아, 아쉬워요. 자주 봤는데.
A: I'm moving next week / B: Oh, that's too bad. We saw each other often.
everyday: regret at parting, politely
A: 비 와서 소풍 취소됐어 / B: 아쉽다. 날씨만 좋았어도.
A: The picnic got canceled because of rain / B: What a shame. If only the weather had held.
real situation: 아쉽다 with a wistful 'if only' follow-up
nuance: 아쉽다 is the mild, wistful 'that's a shame / I wish it were otherwise' — soft regret that something nice didn't happen or is ending, NOT deep sadness. Casual 아쉽다/아쉬워, polite 아쉬워요, in-the-moment 아쉽네(요). The dividing line versus 슬프다 ('sad') and 속상하다 ('upset, distressed') is intensity and cause: 아쉽다 is a gentle 'aw, too bad' about a missed chance or pleasant thing ending; 슬프다 is real sadness (a loss); 속상하다 is being genuinely upset/hurt inside. Missing a sale → 아쉽다; a pet dying → 슬프다; your work being criticized unfairly → 속상하다. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 슬프다 ('sad') for everyday letdowns — to a Korean ear 슬프다 over sold-out tickets is melodramatic; the natural word is 아쉽다. Another is that 아쉽다 can also mean 'to feel a lack / miss having something' (뭔가 아쉽다 'something's missing'), so context decides between 'shame' and 'lacking.'

english: I'm upset / it hurts / it's distressing — genuinely bothered or heartsick about something.
usage: that must be so upsetting for you
examples: A: 키우던 화분이 다 죽었어 / B: 아, 속상하겠다.
A: All my plants died / B: Oh, that must be upsetting.
the bare empathy reaction — feeling for someone
A: 열심히 했는데 결과가 안 좋아서 속상해요.
A: I worked hard but the result was bad, so I'm upset.
everyday: expressing your own hurt politely
A: 애가 말을 안 들어서 너무 속상해요 / B: 속상하시겠어요. 힘드시죠.
A: My kid won't listen, I'm so upset / B: That must be so upsetting. It's hard, isn't it.
real situation: honorific 속상하시겠어요 to comfort an elder
nuance: 속상하다 literally means 'the insides (속) are hurt/spoiled (상하다)' — a heartsick, gnawing upset, the feeling when something genuinely bothers, frustrates, or grieves you inside. Casual 속상해, polite 속상해요, and to empathize with a senior 속상하시겠어요 'that must hurt for you.' The dividing line versus 화나다 ('angry') is direction: 속상하다 is inward hurt/distress (often you're sad-frustrated, maybe near tears), while 화나다 is outward anger at someone. A child ignoring you → 속상하다 (heartache); a rude stranger → 화나다 (anger). The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'upset' as 화나다 — English 'upset' often means hurt/sad, which is 속상하다, not anger. Another pitfall is the empathy form: when comforting someone, native speakers say 속상하겠다 / 속상하시겠어요 ('that must be upsetting for you'), guessing the other's feeling with -겠-; saying just 속상해요 about someone else's situation sounds like you're the one upset.

english: Ugh, so annoying / this is irritating — frustration at something getting on your nerves.
usage: casual banmal, venting to a friend
polite -요, but still informal in flavor
examples: A: 또 에러야 / B: 아, 짜증 나.
A: It's an error again / B: Ugh, so annoying.
the bare vent — irritation at a glitch
A: 버스 또 놓쳤어. 진짜 짜증 나.
A: Missed the bus again. So annoying.
everyday: venting frustration about a daily hassle
A: 옆에서 계속 시끄럽게 해서 짜증 났어 / B: 아, 그럴 만하다.
A: They kept being loud next to me, it got on my nerves / B: Yeah, no wonder.
real situation: 짜증 나다 about something that irritated you over time
nuance: 짜증 나 means 'it's irritating / getting on my nerves' — the prickly frustration of small things piling up (errors, delays, noise). 짜증 is the noun 'irritation/peevishness' and 나(다) is 'arises,' so literally 'irritation arises.' Casual 짜증 나, exclamatory 짜증 난다; the polite 짜증 나요 exists but stays informal and a bit blunt, so you rarely say it to a boss. The dividing line versus 화나다 is degree and color: 짜증 나다 is low-grade peevish annoyance/frustration ('ugh, this again'), while 화나다 is real anger directed at someone. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and spacing: it's 짜증(이) 나다 — 짜증 is the thing that 'comes up,' so don't say 짜증해 (no such verb) or 짜증을 해; if you must mark it, it's 짜증이 나다 or the verb 짜증 내다 ('to act irritated'). Another pitfall is register: even 짜증 나요 sounds too raw to an elder; there, soften to 좀 힘드네요 or 불편하네요.

english: I'm so excited / this is fun / yay — bubbling, happy excitement.
usage: casual exclamatory, to oneself or friends
with 완전 to amp up the excitement
examples: A: 내일 여행 가! / B: 신난다!
A: We go on the trip tomorrow! / B: Yay!
the bare reaction — bubbling excitement
A: 오늘 일찍 끝나서 신나.
A: We finish early today, so I'm excited.
everyday: cheerful about good timing
A: 콘서트 티켓 구했어! / B: 진짜? 신난다! 빨리 가고 싶다.
A: I got the concert tickets! / B: Really? Yay! I can't wait to go.
real situation: 신난다 with 빨리 가고 싶다 to show eager anticipation
nuance: 신난다 is bright, bubbling excitement — 'yay, this is fun, I can't wait!' — the happy buzz before or during something enjoyable. From 신(이) 나다 'spirit/excitement arises': plain 신나, exclamatory 신난다, polite 신나요. The dividing line versus 기대돼요 ('I'm looking forward to it') and 재미있다 ('it's fun/interesting') is the feeling: 신나다 is active, energetic excitement/joy (you're bouncing), 기대되다 is calm anticipation, 재미있다 describes how fun an activity IS. Anticipating a trip with energy → 신난다; quietly looking forward → 기대돼요; describing the trip afterward as fun → 재미있었어. The English-speaker pitfall is using 흥분되다 for 'excited' — 흥분되다 means worked-up/agitated (even aroused or angry) and sounds off for innocent fun; happy excitement is 신나다. Another pitfall is register: 신난다 is breezy and casual, fine with friends, but to express enthusiasm to a superior you'd say 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.

english: Whoa, you scared me! / yikes — startled when something jumps out or surprises you suddenly.
usage: with 아 as the natural gasp lead-in
examples: (친구가 갑자기 등장) A: 야! / B: 아, 깜짝이야!
(friend pops up suddenly) A: Hey! / B: Oh, you scared me!
the bare startle — instant reflex
A: 뒤에서 갑자기 부르지 마, 깜짝이야.
A: Don't call me from behind suddenly, you scared me.
everyday: mild complaint after being startled
A: (문 열다 마주침) 어머! / B: 아, 깜짝이야. 안에 계신 줄 몰랐어요.
A: (opens door, bumps into someone) Oh! / B: Oh, you startled me. I didn't know you were inside.
real situation: startle then polite explanation to someone senior
nuance: 깜짝이야 is the reflex 'whoa, you scared me!' that bursts out the instant something startles you — someone appearing suddenly, a loud noise, a jump-scare. It's from 깜짝 (the mimetic word for a sudden start) + 이야, and it's inherently casual/reflexive; there's no neat polite version of 깜짝이야 itself, so in a respectful setting you switch to the full 깜짝 놀랐어요 'I was startled.' The dividing line versus 무서워 ('I'm scared/afraid') is duration: 깜짝이야 / 깜짝 놀라다 is a momentary jolt of surprise that's over in a second, while 무섭다 is sustained fear/dread (a horror movie, a scary dog). A friend jumping out → 깜짝이야; a dark alley → 무서워. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 너 나를 무섭게 했어 ('you scared me') as a literal translation — that's unnatural; Koreans say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 깜짝이야. Another pitfall is treating 놀라다 as transitive: you don't 'scare someone' with 놀라다 directly; the person 놀라다 (gets startled), and to startle them you say 놀라게 하다.

english: No way / that's ridiculous / unbelievable — strong disbelief at something absurd or shocking.
examples: A: 그 사람이 1등이래 / B: 말도 안 돼.
A: They say that person came first / B: No way.
the bare reaction — flat disbelief
A: 집값이 두 배 올랐대 / B: 말도 안 돼. 어떻게 그래?
A: They say housing prices doubled / B: That's ridiculous. How is that possible?
everyday: disbelief at outrageous news
A: 환불이 안 된다고 하시네요 / B: 네? 말도 안 돼요. 영수증도 있는데요.
A: They're saying no refunds / B: What? That's outrageous. I even have the receipt.
real situation: polite 말도 안 돼요 protesting something unfair
nuance: 말도 안 돼 literally means 'it doesn't even become words' → 'that makes no sense / no way / that's ridiculous,' a strong reaction of disbelief or protest at something absurd, shocking, or unfair. Casual 말도 안 돼, polite 말도 안 돼요. The dividing line versus 진짜? / 정말요? is strength: 진짜? is a light 'really?' that's open to it being true, while 말도 안 돼 flatly rejects it as impossible/outrageous — much stronger. It also differs from 대박 (which is 'wow, huge'); 말도 안 돼 is 'that can't be right.' The English-speaker pitfall is the spacing and negation: it's 말도 안 돼 (안 + 되다 → 안 돼), four parts, and 돼 is spelled 돼 (되+어), never 되; writing 말도 안 되 (no final ㅓ) is a common error. Another pitfall is register/strength — said to a superior 말도 안 돼요 can sound confrontational, so to politely push back you might soften to 그럴 리가요 ('surely not') or 이해가 안 되네요.

structuredNuance.t: 말도 안 돼 is a strong reaction of disbelief or protest at something absurd, shocking, or unfair. Casual 말도 안 돼, polite 말도 안 돼요.
It literally means 'it doesn't even become words' → 'that makes no sense / no way / that's ridiculous.'

mistakes: Writing 말도 안 되 — the form is 말도 안 돼 (되+어 = 돼); as a sentence-final reaction it must end in 돼, not 되.
Using 말도 안 돼(요) for mild surprise — it's strong rejection ('impossible/ridiculous'); for open-minded 'really?' use 진짜? / 정말요?.
Dropping 말도 안 돼요 on a superior in a dispute — it can sound confrontational; to push back politely use 그럴 리가요 or 이해가 안 되네요.

english: Right? / exactly / I know, right — agreeing that you feel the same, often a bit helplessly.
usage: polite -요, agreeing with someone you respect
yeah, right / tell me about it
examples: A: 오늘 진짜 덥다 / B: 그러게.
A: It's really hot today / B: Right?
the bare agreement — echoing a shared feeling
A: 요즘 왜 이렇게 시간이 빨라요 / B: 그러게요, 벌써 6월이에요.
A: Why does time fly these days / B: I know, right — it's June already.
everyday: polite agreement with a mutual observation
A: 그때 그거 샀어야 했는데 / B: 그러게 말이에요. 지금은 품절이래요.
A: We should've bought it back then / B: Exactly. It's sold out now.
real situation: 그러게 말이에요 agreeing with a regret you both share
nuance: 그러게(요) means 'right? / I feel the same' — you AGREE with something the other person just said, often with a faint helpless or regretful tinge ('yeah, I know, what can you do'). Casual 그러게, polite 그러게요, emphatic 그러게 말이에요 'exactly, you said it.' The crucial dividing line is against 그렇구나/그렇군요: 그러게(요) responds to a SHARED feeling or opinion you already had ('I know, right'), while 그렇구나 reacts to NEW information you just learned ('oh, I see, I didn't know that'). So to '오늘 진짜 덥다' you say 그러게요 (I feel it too), but to '나 사실 부산 출신이야' you say 그렇구나 (news to you) — swap them and you sound off. The English-speaker pitfall is using 그러게요 for new facts, which implies you already knew and can seem dismissive. Another pitfall is hearing it as disagreement; it is agreement. To a superior, 그러게요 is fine but 맞아요 / 그러네요 can feel a touch more attentive.

Saying plain 그러게 to a boss or elder — it's banmal; keep the polite 그러게요 (or 그러게 말이에요) with anyone you use 존댓말 with.
Reading 그러게요 as disagreement or doubt — it actually means 'right, I feel the same,' a soft, often resigned agreement.

english: Oh my / oh! — a quick gasp of surprise, more neutral and usable than 헐.
usage: neutral surprise, common (esp. women, all ages)
oh my, what do we do
examples: A: (컵을 떨어뜨림) / B: 어머!
A: (drops a cup) / B: Oh!
the bare gasp — instant surprise
A: 이거 선물이에요 / B: 어머, 뭘 이런 걸 다. 감사해요.
A: This is a gift for you / B: Oh my, you shouldn't have. Thank you.
everyday: pleased-surprised reaction to a gift
A: 비 갑자기 쏟아진다 / B: 어머, 우산도 없는데 어떡해.
A: It's suddenly pouring / B: Oh my, and I don't have an umbrella, what do I do.
real situation: 어머 leads into 어떡해 as surprise turns to worry
nuance: 어머 is a quick, soft gasp of surprise — 'oh!' / 'oh my' — far more neutral and polite-safe than slangy 헐 or 대박, so it works in many settings and across ages. Stronger is 어머나; surprise plus worry is 어머 어떡해. It is a reflexive interjection, so it doesn't take -요, but because it's gentle and non-slang you can use it in front of elders and in semi-formal moments where 헐 would sound rude. The dividing line versus 헐 is register and tone: 헐 is casual youth slang skewing toward shock/dismay, while 어머 is softer, more refined surprise that anyone can use politely. Note the usage skew: 어머/어머나 is used by everyone but especially associated with women's speech; men also reach for 어 / 어이쿠 / 헐 more. The English-speaker pitfall is using only 헐 in every surprised moment, which sounds too slangy with older people — 어머 is the safe, graceful default. Another is over-using it flatly; it carries real emotional color, so it should sound like a genuine gasp.

mistakes: Defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment, including with elders — 헐 is slang and can sound rude; 어머 is the neutral, polite-safe gasp.
Adding -요 as 어머요 — it's a reflexive interjection and doesn't take -요; for politeness, follow it with a full polite sentence.
Treating 어머 as meaningless filler — it carries genuine surprise/emotion, so saying it flatly with no feeling sounds odd; it should sound like a real gasp.
